grammar.title: PAST TENSE REVIEW
points: Past simple = finished actions (single or repeated) at a known past time: We moved to Seville in 2019.
Past continuous = an action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted by a past simple action: I was cooking when the lights went out.

used to + infinitive = past states and habits that are no longer true; would + infinitive = repeated past actions only, never states: I used to have a dog and we would walk for hours. In questions and negatives write did / didn't use to.

Present perfect simple = past actions with no stated time or with a link to now (ever, never, just, already, yet): She's just finished. Present perfect continuous = an activity that began in the past and is still going on: I've been revising since six.

Past perfect simple = an action or state before another past moment: The film had started when we arrived. Past perfect continuous = an activity in progress up to that moment: He was out of breath because he had been running.

grammar.title: COMPARATIVES AND SUPERLATIVES
points: Short adjectives take -er / the -est; longer ones take more / the most (or less / the least): This street is quieter, but that one is more convenient.
Learn the irregular forms: good - better - best, bad - worse - worst, far - further - furthest.
Most adverbs use more / most (more carefully). Adverbs that look like adjectives take -er / -est (faster, harder, earlier). Also well - better - best and badly - worse - worst.

Show the size of a difference with a bit, a little, slightly (small) or much, far, a lot (big): far cheaper. With superlatives use by far or easily: by far the best. For the opposite idea use not as ... as: not as hard as.

Double comparatives show continuing change: It's getting hotter and hotter; more and more expensive. The + comparative, the + comparative shows two things changing together: The earlier we leave, the sooner we'll arrive.

grammar.title: MODAL VERBS: REVIEW
points: Deduction: must + infinitive = you are almost sure it's true; can't = almost sure it's impossible; may / might / could = it's possible: Her light is on, so she must be in.
Permission: ask with can, could or may (could and may are more polite); give it with can and refuse it with can't.

Obligation: must / mustn't for rules and for what the speaker feels is important; have to for obligations that come from outside. mustn't = it's forbidden, but don't have to / needn't = it isn't necessary.
need to / don't need to / needn't express necessity or lack of it. For the future use will have to and will need to.
Advice: should / shouldn't. ought to / ought not to is stronger and suggests a duty: You ought to apologise.

grammar.title: MODALS IN THE PAST
points: Past deduction: must have + past participle (almost sure it happened), can't have (almost sure it didn't), may / might / could have (perhaps it did). For a negative possibility use may not have or might not have.
Past permission: could / couldn't or was / were allowed to: We were allowed to stay up late at weekends.
Past obligation: had to or needed to (must has no past form). didn't have to / didn't need to = it wasn't necessary. needn't have + past participle = you did it, but it turned out to be unnecessary.
should have / ought to have + past participle = criticism or regret about the past: I should have left earlier.
Past ability: could for general abilities (I could swim at five). For one successful action on a specific occasion use was able to or managed to, not could. couldn't works in both cases.

grammar.title: THE FUTURE
points: Present simple for timetables (The ferry sails at nine) and after time words such as when, as soon as, until: I'll text you when I land. Present continuous for fixed arrangements: I'm seeing the dentist on Friday.
will for predictions, future facts, promises, offers, refusals and instant decisions. going to for intentions and for predictions based on something you can see now.
be about to + infinitive = something will happen very soon: Hurry, the film is about to start.

Future continuous (will be + -ing) = in progress at a future time. Future perfect (will have + past participle) = finished before a future time. Future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) = how long something will have lasted by then.
Future in the past: was / were going to (also for plans that never happened) and would: I knew she would win.

grammar.title: GERUNDS AND INFINITIVES
points: Some verbs are followed by to + infinitive: afford, agree, decide, hope, manage, offer, promise, refuse: We agreed to share the bill.
Others are followed by -ing: admit, avoid, consider, deny, enjoy, finish, keep, miss, risk, suggest, can't stand, look forward to: He keeps interrupting.

begin, start and continue take both forms with no real change. forget, remember, stop, try, go on and mean change meaning: I remembered to lock the door (I didn't forget) but I remember locking it (I have the memory).
Adjective + to-infinitive (happy to help, hard to say); adjective + preposition + -ing (good at drawing, tired of waiting).
Use -ing after every preposition (before leaving, without asking) and as the subject of a sentence: Swimming keeps me fit.

grammar.title: CONDITIONALS
points: Zero: if + present, present = something that is always true: If you press this, it beeps. When the if clause comes first, put a comma after it.
First: if + present, will / may / might = a likely future result. unless means if not: We'll be late unless we run.
Second: if + past simple, would / could + infinitive = an unlikely or imaginary present or future: If I were you, I'd apologise.
Third: if + past perfect, would / might / could have + past participle = an imaginary past: If we had booked, we would have got seats.

Mixed: past cause with present result = if + past perfect, would + infinitive (If I had slept more, I wouldn't be tired now). Present fact with past result = if + past simple, would have + past participle (If I spoke French, I'd have got the job).

grammar.title: WISH AND IF ONLY
points: wish + past simple or past continuous = you are unhappy about a present situation: I wish I had a bigger room.
wish + past perfect = regret about the past: I wish I had brought a coat.
wish + could + infinitive = something you would like to be able to do but find difficult: I wish I could dance.

wish + would / wouldn't = you are irritated by someone else's behaviour or by a situation and want it to change: I wish they would turn the music down. Don't use it about yourself (not I wish I would).

grammar.title: CLEFT SENTENCES
points: A cleft sentence splits one idea into two parts so that one piece of information stands out.
What-clause + is / was + noun phrase: What I need is a holiday. You can also begin with All: All I want is some peace.
What + subject + do / did + is / was + infinitive emphasises an action: What she did was call the police. After verbs like want or intend keep to: What I want is to sleep.
It + is / was + emphasised part + that / who clause: It was Marta who found the keys.
With It-clefts you can highlight a person, a thing, a time or a place: It was in Rome that we met; It was last week that he called.

It was my brother ____ broke the window. (who / which) | who

grammar.title: INVERSION
points: In formal or dramatic style, a negative or limiting expression at the start of a sentence is followed by question word order (auxiliary + subject + verb): Never have I seen such a mess.
Negative starters: never, not once, at no time, under no circumstances, no way, not since, not only ... but also.
Limiting starters: little, rarely, seldom, hardly, only then, only when, not until.
If the normal sentence has no auxiliary, add do / does / did: Rarely does he complain; Little did we know.
After only when / not until + clause, the inversion comes in the main clause: Not until I got home did I notice the stain.

grammar.title: THE PASSIVE
points: Form: be in the right tense + past participle. Only verbs that can take an object have a passive. Use it to focus on the person or thing affected: The bridge was built in 1900.
It works in all tenses and after modals: is being repaired, has been sold, had been stolen, will be sent, must be signed.
In informal English get can replace be: My bike got stolen.
The object of the active sentence becomes the passive subject; the doer can be added with by: The goal was scored by Lucia.
Leave the agent out when it is obvious, unknown or secret: Two men were arrested last night.

grammar.title: PASSIVE GERUND & INFINITIVE
points: Verbs that take a to-infinitive take the passive infinitive to be + past participle (She hopes to be chosen); verbs that take -ing take being + past participle (He avoids being seen).
Use to be + past participle after adjectives: I was glad to be invited.
Use be + past participle after modal verbs: The flight might be cancelled.
Use being + past participle after prepositions and as the subject of a sentence: I'm tired of being ignored; Being chosen was an honour.
Verbs with two objects (give, send, offer, show, tell, teach, lend, pay) have two passives: I was given a prize / A prize was given to me. Making the person the subject usually sounds more natural.
questions: I hate ____ (tell) what to do. | being told

grammar.title: CAUSATIVES
points: have + object + past participle = you arrange for somebody else to do a job: I had my bike repaired. The same pattern describes bad things that happen to you: She had her phone stolen.
get + object + past participle means the same but is more informal: I must get my jacket cleaned.
get + person + to-infinitive = ask or persuade somebody: I got my sister to help. have + person + infinitive without to is more formal: I'll have the porter carry your bags.
make + person + infinitive without to = force somebody: The coach made us run ten laps.
let + person + infinitive without to = allow somebody: Mum let me stay up late.

grammar.title: REPORTED SPEECH
points: Tenses usually move one step back (am - was, have done - had done, did - had done, will - would, can - could). The past perfect, would, could and should stay the same. The word that is optional.
No tense change is needed if the words are still true or if the reporting verb is in the present: She says she's tired.
Pronouns, possessives and time or place words change: tomorrow - the next day, yesterday - the day before, here - there, ago - before.

Reporting verbs have their own patterns: verb + to-infinitive (agree, offer, promise); verb + object + to-infinitive (advise, invite, tell, persuade, warn); verb + -ing (suggest, recommend, deny, admit); verb + preposition + -ing (apologise for, insist on, complain about).
To report what people in general say, use It + passive: It is believed that the painting is a fake.

grammar.title: RELATIVE CLAUSES
points: who / that for people, which / that for things, whose for possession, where for places, when for times, why for reasons. whom is formal and used after prepositions.
Defining clauses give essential information and have no commas. When the pronoun is the object of the clause you can drop it: The film (that) we saw was great.
Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas. Never use that in them and never drop the pronoun: My aunt, who lives in Cádiz, is a nurse.
which can refer back to a whole clause to add a comment: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.
Prepositions: formal style puts them before the pronoun (the person to whom I spoke); everyday style puts them at the end (the person I spoke to).

grammar.title: PARTICIPLE CLAUSES
points: Present participle (-ing) clauses describe an action at the same time as, or just before, the main action, or its result: Opening the door, she saw a stranger. Both parts must share the same subject.
They can follow conjunctions and prepositions such as while, after, before, since, on: After leaving school, he moved abroad.
Perfect participle clauses (having + past participle) show that one action was complete before the next, often giving a reason: Having lost my keys, I couldn't get in.
Past participle clauses have a passive meaning: Built in 1900, the house needs repairs.

Participles can replace relative clauses (the girl sitting by the window; the cars made here) and reason clauses (Being tired, I went to bed). Make them negative with not: Not knowing the answer, I guessed.
